treatment.organic_subtitle: Organic, cultural, and biological methods to restore your crop safely.
prevention.subtitle: Simple preventive steps for your field to stop future recurrence.
chemical.warning: Consider chemical treatment only when organic methods are insufficient, strictly according to the product label and local agricultural guidance. Always wear protective gear.
symptom.tomato_early_blight_1: Dark brown to black concentric circular spots resembling a target board on older leaves.
symptom.tomato_early_blight_2: Yellow halo surrounding the circular brown lesions.
symptom.tomato_early_blight_3: Gradual drying and premature falling of lower foliage.
organic.tomato_early_blight_t1_desc: Carefully pinch off and safely burn or bury heavily infected leaves. Never place them in compost piles.
organic.tomato_early_blight_t2_desc: Mix 50ml neem oil or NSKE with 10 liters of water and mild soap. Spray during cool morning hours over leaves.
organic.tomato_early_blight_t3_desc: Spread dry straw or plastic mulch around the plant base to prevent soil fungi from splashing onto leaves during watering.
prevention.tomato_early_blight_p1_desc: Do not plant tomatoes, potatoes, or eggplants in the same field plot for at least two consecutive seasons.
prevention.tomato_early_blight_p2_desc: Apply water directly at soil level. Keeping leaf foliage dry prevents fungal spores from germinating.
chemical.tomato_early_blight_title: Mancozeb 75% WP or Copper Oxychloride 50% WP
chemical.tomato_early_blight_desc: Dissolve 2g to 2.5g per liter of clean water. Apply only if disease exceeds 20% leaf area and organic remedies have failed.
symptom.potato_late_blight_1: Water-soaked irregular pale to dark green lesions turning rapidly brownish-black.
symptom.potato_late_blight_2: White delicate mold growth on the underside of leaves during humid mornings.
symptom.potato_late_blight_3: Foul rotting odor in severely affected potato field patches.
organic.potato_late_blight_t1_desc: Immediately uproot infected plants showing severe stem rot and deep bury outside field boundaries.
organic.potato_late_blight_t2_desc: Apply Trichoderma viride or Pseudomonas fluorescens formulation (10g/L) to soil and foliar canopy to suppress blight spores.
organic.potato_late_blight_t3_desc: Build high soil ridges around potato stems to stop spores washing down into developing tubers during rainfall.
prevention.potato_late_blight_p1_desc: Only plant certified clean seed potatoes from recognized agricultural departments.
prevention.potato_late_blight_p2_desc: Ensure standard row spacing of 60cm x 20cm to permit maximum sunlight penetration and quick drying.
chemical.potato_late_blight_desc: Foliar spray at 2.5g per liter. Use strictly with advice from your local Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK).
symptom.paddy_blast_1: Spindle-shaped or eye-shaped lesions with grayish-white centers and brownish margins.
symptom.paddy_blast_2: Lesions enlarge and coalesce, causing entire leaf blades to wither and scorch.
symptom.paddy_blast_3: Blackening and breaking of the node at panicle base (neck blast) during grain filling.
organic.paddy_blast_t1_desc: Dilute 300ml authentic fermented Panchagavya in 10 liters water and spray evenly across the crop canopy.
organic.paddy_blast_t2_desc: Avoid excessive chemical urea fertilizer. Split nitrogen doses and incorporate farmyard manure or neem cake.
prevention.paddy_blast_p1_desc: Treat seeds with Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 10g/kg seed before nursery sowing.
prevention.paddy_blast_p2_desc: Maintain thin layer of water; avoid drought stress in field as moisture deficit makes plants vulnerable.
chemical.paddy_blast_desc: Spray at 0.6g per liter water at early tillering or heading stage only when blast lesions are actively spreading.
symptom.chilli_leaf_curl_1: Upward curling, puckering, and reduction in leaf size.
symptom.chilli_leaf_curl_2: Stunted bushy plant growth with shortened internodes.
symptom.chilli_leaf_curl_3: Poor flowering and small deformed fruits.
organic.chilli_leaf_curl_t1_desc: Spray organic Agniastra or garlic-chilli-ginger extract to repel sap-sucking whitefly vectors.
organic.chilli_leaf_curl_t2_desc: Install 12 yellow sticky traps per acre at canopy height to capture whiteflies naturally.
prevention.chilli_leaf_curl_p1_title: Border Crop of Maize or Sorghum
prevention.chilli_leaf_curl_p1_desc: Plant 2 to 3 dense rows of maize or sorghum around chilli fields as a live barrier against incoming vectors.
chemical.chilli_leaf_curl_desc: Target whiteflies with labeled systemic insecticide only as emergency intervention under severe infestation.
symptom.healthy_1: Vibrant natural green coloration across all leaf veins.
symptom.healthy_2: Smooth blade structure without spots, lesions, or curling.
symptom.healthy_3: Vigorous growth with no signs of fungal or bacterial infection.
organic.healthy_t1_desc: Add compost, jeevamrutha, or decomposed cow dung to sustain strong roots and natural immunity.
organic.healthy_t2_desc: Keep consistent moisture without waterlogging root zones.
prevention.healthy_p1_desc: Walk your field twice a week early morning to spot any early leaf discoloration before it spreads.
prevention.healthy_p2_desc: Plant marigold borders to deter pests and attract beneficial pollinator insects.
chemical.healthy_none_desc: Your plant is in great health. Avoid applying unnecessary chemical pesticides to preserve natural predators.
chemical.general_precautions: Safety rules: Always wear protective rubber gloves and mask. Keep away from water bodies and animals. Observe waiting period before harvest.

help.title: Farmer Support & Guide
help.q1: How do I take a good photo of an infected leaf?
help.a1: Hold the camera steady about 10-15cm away from the leaf. Ensure sunlight is falling directly on the spots, and avoid heavy shadows.
help.q2: Why does ILAI SCAN show organic treatments first?
help.a2: Organic and cultural methods cost less, protect soil health, preserve beneficial insects, and avoid chemical toxicity for your family.
help.q3: When should I consult an expert?
help.a3: If confidence is below 80% or if disease spreads rapidly across more than a quarter of your field, visit your nearest KVK or agricultural officer.
